check.population: every schema, type, name and stored fact that represents one concept
check.freshness: a verdict stands until a schema, a type or a stored representation changes
check.refusal: the type checker, schema registry or validation pipeline fails a representation that diverges from the canonical one
check.observation: schemas and types compared across producers, stores and consumers of the same concept
check.evidence: none: the catalog states this check as a class, so a watched run belongs to each system that adopts it
check.authority: the canonical representation, which every producer, store and consumer conforms to

records.name: Schema Validation
records.definition: A mechanism that parses incoming data against a schema at the boundary and rejects any payload that does not conform.

exemplar.after:
const FooSchema = object({ id: string(), name: string().min(1), count: integer().min(0) });
const foo = FooSchema.parse(JSON.parse(raw));

distinctFrom.reason: Type safety rejects wrongly typed operations at compile time, while compile-time evaluation runs computations and checks during the build.

records.name: Type Safety
records.definition: A mechanism that has the compiler reject operations on values of the wrong type before the code runs.

exemplar.before:
function loadFoo(id: string): any { return fooStore.get(id); }
const count = loadFoo("x").coutn + 1;

records.name: Canonical Model
records.definition: A design rule that a concept has one authoritative representation, and every other representation is translated to and from it.

records.name: Canonical Data Model
records.definition: A design pattern in which integrated systems exchange data through one shared model, with a mapping per system.

exemplar.before:
fooTable.insert({ foo_id: foo.id, foo_name: foo.name });
barTable.insert({ id: foo.id, label: foo.name });

records.name: Canonical Schema
records.definition: A formal definition of one concept's shape, published once and used by every API, message and store that carries the concept.

exemplar.before:
const fooSchema = { id: "string", name: "string" };
const barFooSchema = { fooId: "text", label: "text" };

records.name: Canonicalization
records.definition: A technique for converting equivalent values to one normal form before they are compared, stored or checked.

exemplar.before:
const keys = ["Foo", " foo ", "FOO"];
const map = new Map(keys.map(key => [key, loadFoo(key)]));
exemplar.after:
function canonicalFooKey(value: string) { return value.trim().normalize("NFKC").toLowerCase(); }
const map = new Map(keys.map(key => [canonicalFooKey(key), loadFoo(canonicalFooKey(key))]));

distinctFrom.reason: A single source of truth gives each fact one owner, while a canonical model gives a concept one representation that others translate to and from.
A single source of truth owns each fact once, while a closed vocabulary limits the words a name slot may hold.
A single source of truth is one owner per fact, while collision consolidation reads a taken filename as evidence of two files doing one job.
A single source of truth is one owner per fact, while declared jurisdiction is the declaration a naming gate reads its scope from.
A single source of truth owns facts, rules and configuration values, while DRY keeps one source for logic and constants in code.
A single source of truth centralizes ownership of a fact, while decentralization spreads decisions and control to the owning teams.
A single source of truth fixes where a fact lives, while determinism fixes that the same inputs give the same result.
A single source of truth owns facts, while governance holds decisions to policy.

records.name: Single Source of Truth
records.definition: A design rule that each fact, rule or configuration value has one owning definition, and every other value is derived from it.

records.name: Normalization
records.definition: A technique for storing each fact once and referring to it by key wherever it is needed.

exemplar.before:
type Foo = { id: FooId; barName: string; barEmail: string };
const foos: Foo[] = duplicateBarAcrossFoos();

distinctFrom.reason: Semantic consistency is one name keeping one meaning, while polysemy across contexts is a term legitimately meaning different things in different bounded contexts.

records.name: Semantic Consistency
records.definition: The degree to which one name carries one meaning across the code, the schemas and the documentation.

records.name: Ubiquitous Language
records.definition: The practice of using the domain's own terms, agreed with its experts, in conversation, documentation and code alike.

distinctFrom.reason: An intent-revealing interface states what an operation does in its name and parameters, while least surprise requires the behavior to match what they lead a caller to expect.

records.name: Intent-Revealing Interface
records.definition: A design rule that an operation's name and parameters state what it does for the caller.

records.name: Principle of Least Surprise
records.definition: A design rule that an operation behaves the way its name and its conventions lead a caller to expect.

exemplar.after:
function getFoo(id: FooId) { return fooStore.find(id); }
function deleteFoo(id: FooId) { return fooStore.delete(id); }

records.name: Database Normalization
records.definition: A technique for decomposing tables by their functional dependencies into normal forms, so no column depends on anything but its key.
detected_by: the same fact stored in multiple places drifting out of sync
